title: Will You Be Bitter or Better
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Drawing on a phrase from motivational speaker Josh Shipp, this article frames the aftermath of any setback as a binary choice: let the event curdle into bitterness, or use it as fuel to grow stronger. The author argues this choice is less about finding a silver lining than about deciding how much power to give the negative event over one's ongoing attitude and actions. The piece assigns leaders a specific role in this process — modeling their own past struggles with resentment and gently nudging others toward the constructive path rather than lecturing them into it.
points: After any significant setback, people face a defining choice between bitterness and growth.
The choice is not about denying the hardship but about limiting how much negative control the event is allowed to have.
It is easier to see this clearly from the outside than to apply it when the setback is one's own.
Good leaders help others make this choice by sharing their own past struggles with resentment rather than being preachy.
The article closes with Zig Ziglar's line that attitude, not aptitude, determines altitude.
quotes: Will they choose to allow this event to make them “bitter or better?” as motivational speaker Josh Shipp likes to say.
Rather, it is about choosing how much negative control we allow the situation to have.
Those who surrender themselves to the disappointment quickly become victims of their own demise.
At the moment bitterness begins to take hold, people need the help of leaders to make a different decision.
Good leaders go out of their way to remind us that better is more powerful than bitter in tough situations.
